summary: Inconsistent rate-limit headers and apparent token double-counting during multiplexed websocket + HTTP upload workload
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports receiving 429 responses for a subset of requests even though the X-RateLimit-* headers returned in prior responses implied available quota. The workload is a mix of long-lived websocket streams (chat-style) and short-lived HTTP POST chunked uploads for document ingestion.

Impact:
- Intermittent 429s for streaming clients after a period of bulk ingestion (customer-visible errors).
- Clients report header values (X-RateLimit-Remaining/X-RateLimit-Reset) that do not match subsequent immediate 429 status.
- Customer cannot reliably separate streaming vs bulk traffic due to tenant-level token accounting; this threatens their SLA for real-time features.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated GPU farm) in us-east.
- Traffic through Redwood edge-proxy fronting HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and websocket upgrades on the same IPs.
- Mixed API key usage: single API key reused by ingest workers and streaming clients.

Observed behavior:
1) Start ~20 long-lived streaming websocket sessions (low token rate).
2) Kick off concurrent multipart HTTP uploads from ~50 short-lived workers.
3) Within 30–120s some streaming clients receive 429s with headers indicating non-zero Remaining tokens in previous responses.

Expected behavior:
- Rate headers should reflect per-tenant accounting and be coherent with immediate acceptance/rejection decisions.
- Streaming sessions should not see sudden 429s when tenant-level tokens are sufficient or when headers indicate remaining allowance.

Workaround requested: guidance on configuration and mitigations until root cause is fixed.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Using dedicated tenant on us-east, open 20 websocket streaming sessions to /v1/chat/stream with same API key.
2) Start 50 parallel HTTP/2 POST multipart uploads to /v1/ingest with same API key; each upload does 10 concurrent chunks.
3) Observe client-side logs for any 429 responses on websocket connections and check X-RateLimit-* headers on both accepted and rejected requests.
4) Repeat with separate API keys for streaming and uploads to compare behavior.

comments: Support (Maya): Logged ticket after initial report from customer. Asked for request IDs and timeline. Provided immediate mitigations: recommend separating API keys for streaming and bulk ingestion and reducing chunk parallelism.
Customer (HelioSearch): Confirmed separation decreased but did not eliminate 429s. Provided pcap and a list of request ids where headers reported Remaining>0 shortly before 429s.
SRE (Arjun): Triaged and pulled edge-proxy traces and rate-limiter metrics. Noted an aggregation mismatch in request attribution between HTTP/2 connection-level counters and per-request accounting.
SRE (Arjun): Requested an experiment window to turn on detailed per-request accounting in prod for the tenant for 1 hour to collect fine-grained traces.
investigation_notes: Initial hypothesis: per-connection accounting for HTTP/2 + websocket upgrade was being cached at the edge and not reconciled with per-request token consumption, causing stale X-RateLimit-Remaining headers to be emitted.

Trace analysis: correlation between 429 events and connection reuse across multiplexed streams (HTTP/2) showed that the edge code path emitted headers from a connection-level snapshot that wasn't updated after concurrent chunked POSTs finished.
Metric evidence: spikes in metric edge.rateheader.stale_count coincident with customer bulk-ingest windows. CPU and serving-runtime metrics normal. No model OOMs or GPU shortages found.

Repro attempt: using a local cluster with HTTP/2 multiplexing we reproduced header mismatch when a health-check thread and chunked uploads incremented the same connection-level counter between header emission and final accounting commit.

Related artifacts: slack thread #support-helio (https://slack.redwood/support-helio), dashboard: https://grafana.redwood/tenant/helio-42/rate-accounting, and traces: https://jaeger.redwood/trace/abc123
Linked code area: edge-proxy header cache and rate-limiter attribution (see pr link below).
resolution:
Mitigation applied: turned off connection-level header caching and switched the tenant to per-request authoritative accounting for the 2-hour experiment window. Immediate effect: streaming clients no longer observed 429s in the test window.

Short-term recommendation to customer:
- Use separate API keys for streaming vs ingestion (we provided a script to rotate keys).
- Reduce parallel chunk concurrency to 4 per worker for now.
- Implement client-side exponential backoff with jitter as documented in our SDK guidelines.

Planned long-term fix: patch edge-proxy to decouple header emission from cached connection snapshots and add atomic commit semantics so headers reflect post-accounting consumptions. Patch submitted: PR #9876. QA plan: canary release to 10% of edge-proxy fleet, verify metrics edge.rateheader.stale_count drops to 0 and no regression in latency.

Follow-up: monitor for 72 hours and schedule a postmortem with HelioSearch; include changes in rate-limiter runbook.
